Remortgaging When You Have Other Debt

When you remortgage, your other borrowing and your mortgage finally meet. It's where the biggest avoidable mistakes get made, and most of them come from rushing.

If your fixed rate is coming to an end and you're carrying other borrowing too, it's worth pausing before you do anything. A remortgage is the moment your loans and your mortgage meet. For most households it's also the largest financial decision they'll make without advice. Both of those facts are a reason to slow down.

Start here: what are you actually remortgaging for?

Three different jobs get called "remortgaging", and they have different right answers.

  1. Rate only. Your fix is ending and you want another one. Same balance, same term. Usually straightforward, and usually worth doing.
  2. Rate plus a bit more borrowing for something specific, like an extension or a new roof. Reasonable, and priced as additional lending.
  3. Rate plus clearing unsecured debt. This is the consequential one. It has its own guide, because the monthly saving is real, and so are two costs that aren't obvious.

It's worth being honest with yourself about which one you're doing. Job three dressed up as job one is how people end up with a thirty-year commitment they never deliberately chose.

The timing that saves the most money

Two dates govern everything: the day your early repayment charge ends, and the day your fixed rate ends. They're usually the same date, but not always, and the gap between them is worth knowing about.

  • Leaving during the fix normally triggers an early repayment charge, commonly one to five per cent of the balance. On a substantial mortgage that's thousands of pounds, and it will usually swamp any saving.
  • Falling off the fix onto the standard variable rate is the expensive default. The SVR is typically well above anything you could arrange for yourself, and lenders aren't obliged to remind you.
  • The window is the three to six months before your fix ends. Most offers stay valid for that long, so you can secure a rate early and complete on the day the fix expires. No early repayment charge, and no month on the SVR.

Put the date your fix ends in a calendar now, with a reminder six months before it. That one small act is worth more than most rate-shopping.

What has changed since you last did this

A remortgage is a full application, not a formality, and things that were fine five years ago may not be fine now:

  • Your commitments. Car finance or loans you've taken on since last time reduce what you can borrow. The arithmetic applies to a remortgage exactly as it does to a purchase.
  • Your income shape. Moving from employment to self-employment is the big one. Most lenders want to see two or three years of accounts.
  • Your property's value. Lenders price by the share of your home's value you're borrowing. They call that share loan-to-value, or LTV, and they price it in bands. If prices have risen, your LTV has improved, and you may reach a cheaper band without doing anything. If they've fallen, the reverse is true. In the worst case there's no equity to remortgage against at all.
  • Your age against the term. Lenders cap the age at which the mortgage must end. That cap can force a shorter term, and a shorter term means a higher monthly payment.

Check your LTV band before you shop. Take a current estimate of what your home is worth, and divide the outstanding balance by it. Then see which side of a band boundary you're on. If you're just the wrong side, a modest lump sum off the balance before you apply can move you into a cheaper band, and the cheaper rate applies to the whole mortgage. It's the highest-return small payment available to you at this moment.

A product transfer versus a full remortgage

Your existing lender will offer you a new deal without you going anywhere. That offer is called a product transfer. There's usually no valuation, minimal paperwork, often no fresh affordability assessment, and it's quick.

It's genuinely useful in two situations. The first is when your circumstances have got worse, and you might not pass a fresh assessment elsewhere. The second is when you simply want the thing done. The cost is that you're choosing from one lender's range without knowing what the rest of the market would have offered, and over a fixed period the difference is frequently substantial.

The sensible approach is to get the product transfer offer, then compare it properly against the open market on total cost over the fixed period rather than on the rate. The fee analyser does exactly this comparison, because a fee-free transfer can beat a lower rate that arrives with a large product fee.

The sequence

  1. Six months out: find the date your fix ends and where you stand on early repayment charges. Get your credit files, and fix anything wrong on them.
  2. Five months out: stop applying for credit. Start bringing card balances down.
  3. Four months out: work out your LTV, and whether a lump sum would cross a band. Decide whether clearing debt is part of this remortgage, deliberately and on paper.
  4. Three months out: get your lender's product transfer offer, and compare the market against it on total cost. Think about a broker too. On a remortgage with any complication, they usually earn their fee.
  5. Secure the offer, timed to complete as the fix ends.
  6. Change nothing between offer and completion.

If the real reason you're remortgaging is that the payments have become genuinely unmanageable, that's a different problem, and a remortgage may not be the answer. Start here instead, and speak to your lender before you miss anything, because the options available before arrears are much better than the ones after.
